questions.prompt: What does adding loading.tsx to a route folder do?

options.text: Shows that UI instantly while the route loads, via a Suspense boundary
Blocks the route from rendering until data is ready

questions.explanation: loading.tsx is shown immediately while the segment loads; Next.js wraps the page in a React <Suspense> with loading.tsx as the fallback.

questions.prompt: Which React component do you wrap a slow widget in to stream it with a fallback? Type the component name.
questions.explanation: <Suspense fallback={...}> shows the fallback until its children finish loading, streaming that subtree independently.

questions.prompt: Why is wrapping an entire page in one Suspense boundary usually wrong?

options.text: The whole page waits on its slowest child, hiding fast content
Suspense can only wrap a single element
It forces the page to render on the client

questions.explanation: A single page-wide boundary makes all content wait on the slowest child. Scope boundaries to the slow subtree instead.

questions.prompt: Which statements about streaming are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The server can send HTML in chunks as parts become ready
It requires a separate backend server you write yourself

questions.explanation: Streaming sends HTML progressively, improving perceived performance, and fallbacks should be light. It's built into Next.js — no separate backend.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to its scope.

pairs.right: A loading state for the whole route segment
Send HTML shell first, slow parts later

questions.explanation: loading.tsx covers a route, Suspense scopes to a subtree, streaming sends HTML progressively, and a fallback is the placeholder.

questions.prompt: Order what the user experiences with a streamed Suspense section.

items.text: The page shell and fast content render immediately
The Suspense fallback shows for the slow section
The slow component's data resolves on the server
The finished section streams in, replacing the fallback

questions.explanation: Streaming shows the shell first, displays the fallback for the slow part, then swaps in that part once its data resolves.
